cover_design.ringkas: A self-study course in Sundanese for complete beginners — from the speech levels that decide whether you sound polite or rude, to the Sundanese script on Bandung's street signs.
cover_design.catatan: Every line of dialogue comes with a word-for-word translation and a stress-marked pronunciation guide.

product.title: Sundanese 101 - A1 (English Edition)
product.description: Twenty Assimil-style self-study units that take you from zero to A1 Sundanese, the language of some 32 million people in West Java: short dialogues, word-for-word translations, grammar notes, vocabulary with an English-friendly pronunciation guide, exercises, and an answer key. The grammar is friendly — no conjugation, no gender, no cases, no plural endings. The real challenge lies elsewhere, and this book puts it front and center from Unit 1: undak usuk basa, the speech-level system that gives one verb three forms (dahar — neda — tuang), where picking the wrong one is not a grammar slip but a breach of manners. Along the way you'll get the eu sound that English doesn't have, the little particles mah, téh, atuh, and geuning that give a sentence its flavor, the tricky words that mean something quite different in Indonesian (bujur, amis, gering, sok, mangga), and a full unit on the Sundanese script, so Bandung's street signs stop being pictures. The dialogues follow Rani, a newcomer from Jakarta settling into Bandung, through ordinary things: bargaining at the market, catching a minibus to Dago, being made to eat at the neighbors', and saying the wrong word in front of her landlady.

blocks.text: Sundanese is the language of West Java — of Bandung, Bogor, Garut, and the green volcanic highlands around them. Around thirty-two million people speak it, making it the third-largest language of Indonesia after Javanese and Indonesian itself, and it is the language you will hear in Bandung's lanes, markets, and living rooms the moment you step away from the shopping malls.

Its grammar is a gift to the beginner. There is no conjugation: a verb never changes for "I", "you", or "they", nor for past or future. There is no grammatical gender, no case, no plural ending. Word order is subject–verb–object, like English. Prefixes and suffixes exist, but they follow clear patterns that you will learn one at a time.
So what is there to learn in twenty units? Three things, and none of them can be guessed.

**First, undak usuk basa — the speech levels.** This is the heart of the course. Sundanese doesn't have one word for "eat" — it has three: *dahar*, *neda*, *tuang*. They are not synonyms but three levels of politeness, chosen according to who is eating and who you are talking to. Choose wrong and your sentence doesn't just sound odd; you sound rude, or so over-refined that it's comic. English has nothing like this system, and it is what gives away even people who have lived in Bandung for ten years.

**Second, tricky words.** Sundanese shares hundreds of words with Indonesian, the national language you'll see on every sign and hear on every TV — and many of them mean something different. *Bujur* is "true" in Indonesian but "buttocks" in Sundanese. *Amis* is "sweet" here, not "fishy-smelling". *Gering* means sick, not skinny. *Sok* means "please, go ahead", not "show-offy". Even if you've only picked up a little Indonesian, these will catch you, so this course collects them one by one, with the full list at the back.

**Third, particles.** *Mah*, *téh*, *atuh*, *waé*, *geuning*, *apan*, *téa* — little words with no dictionary meaning that set the whole feel of a sentence, the way "well", "just", "though", and "come on" do in English. People who use them well sound like they're from Bandung; people who never use them sound like they're reading a translation.

The dialogues follow Rani, a newcomer from Jakarta who has just moved to Bandung for work. She says the wrong word in Unit 3, gets laughed at in Unit 6, and by Unit 20 can sit in a neighbor's front room without making anyone uncomfortable. Her journey is deliberately ordinary, because that is how languages are really learned: in the minibus, at the food stall, in the living room — not in a classroom.

One last word. Sundanese is a big language, but the number of its speakers falls every year, as more and more Sundanese children grow up speaking Indonesian. Everyone who learns it — including you, who are not Sundanese — helps hold that decline back. *Wilujeng diajar* — happy learning.
Every unit is built in the same order, and the order isn't decoration — it follows the way a language gets into an adult's head: listen first, understand next, use last.

items: **Dialogue.** Read it twice. The first time, don't look at the translation at all — let most of it go over your head; that's normal and intended. The second time, read it with the English translation alongside. The *literal* line beneath shows the Sundanese word order as it is, and that line is what teaches you how the language thinks.
**Notes (Catetan).** Explanations of the new words and customs in the dialogue. This is the part you'll most often need to reread.
**Grammar (Tata basa).** One or two grammar points per unit, no more — chosen because they are the ones that actually trip learners up.
**Topic sections.** The theme of the unit, extended: word lists, tables, boxes of ready-made sentences.
**Vocabulary.** Twenty to thirty core words for the unit, each with a pronunciation guide.
**Exercises & answer key.** Four sets of exercises with answers. In the Linguo app you can do them right on the screen.

blocks.text: **Tap any word to hear it.** In the Linguo e-book reader, every Sundanese word can be tapped to be read aloud. An honest warning: the voice engine available for Sundanese has an Indonesian accent, so it doesn't pronounce **eu** quite right. For that sound, trust the explanation in the pronunciation chapter and Unit 2, not the machine.

**Recommended pace: one unit every two days.** Day one, the dialogue and notes; day two, the topic sections and exercises. Twenty units take about six weeks. Going faster than that is usually not learning, just reading.
**Don't skip Unit 3.** It covers the speech levels in full, and every unit after it depends on it. If there is one unit to read three times, it's Unit 3.

The good news: modern Sundanese is written in the Latin alphabet, and spelling is very regular — each letter has one sound. The part that needs attention: there are **seven** vowel sounds, two of which don't exist in English. Master those and ninety percent of your pronunciation is right.
Seven vowels, not five
Sundanese has **seven** vowel sounds, and three of them are written with the letter *e*. The "Say it" column in every vocabulary list spells each sound one consistent way:

blocks.title: How to say eu — a thirty-second exercise
items: Say **oo** as in *food*: your lips round and push forward.
Keep your tongue exactly where it is, and **pull your lips back flat**, as if starting to smile.
The sound that comes out is **eu**. It sounds dull, deep, and a little swallowed — close to the *u* in *put* said with flat lips.
Practice with these three words until they feel natural: **beuki** (more and more), **seueur** (many), **hideung** (black).
The most common mistake: saying *eu* as two separate sounds, *e-u* ("uh-oo"). It is **one** sound, one beat, one syllable.

blocks.text: é and e — they change the meaning
In carefully written Sundanese, *é* always carries its accent mark and *e* never does. This isn't a matter of style: the two sounds are different, and many words exist with only one of them.

In this book the *é* mark is **always** written. In the outside world — signboards, WhatsApp messages, banners — it often disappears, and readers guess from context. After a few units you'll be able to guess too.
Consonants
Most consonants sound as in English. **c** is always *ch* as in *church* (*cai*, water = chah-EE); **j** as in *jam*; **g** is always hard as in *go*; **r** is a light tap or trill. A few more notes:

items: **ny** and **ng** are single sounds: *ny* as in *canyon*, *ng* as in *singer* (never *finger*) — and both can start a word: *nyaho* (to know), *ngomong* (to talk).

**f**, **v**, **z**, and **sy** (*sh*) aren't native to Sundanese. In loanwords, older speakers replace them: *fikir* → *pikir*, *televisi* → *telepisi*, *zaman* → *jaman*, *syukur* → *sukur*. You don't have to copy this, but you will hear it.

**h** at the end of a syllable is clearly breathed out and must not be dropped: *imah* (house), *bohong* (lie), *tuhu* (loyal). Swallow the *h* and you get a different word: *imah* → *ima*. In the "Say it" column, a final *h* after a vowel already spelled with *h* is written **hh**: *imah* = ee-MAHH, *téh* = tehh.

blocks.text: Word stress

Sundanese stress falls on the **last syllable**, unlike English, which tends to stress an earlier one. English speakers want to say *I-mah*; Sundanese speakers say *ee-MAHH*, *dah-HAHR*, *kah-SEHP*, with the peak at the end, so sentences seem to rise as they finish. Copying this rising pattern is the fastest way to make your Sundanese sound Sundanese, even before you know many words. In the "Say it" column, the stressed syllable is in CAPITALS.

blocks.title: Five words to practice everything at once
items: **seueur** — *seu-EUR* — many. Two *eu* sounds in a row.
**heureuy** — *heu-REUY* — to joke. Three dull sounds in a row.
**beureum** — *beu-REUM* — red.
**hideung** — *hee-DEUNG* — black.
**geulis** — *GEU-lees* — pretty. Often the first word newcomers learn, and often mispronounced *guh-oo-lees*.

blocks.text: Two have no counterpart in English (or Indonesian): **-eun** (*daharaneun* = something to eat, *inumeun* = a drink, *pilakadareun* = pitiful) and the plural infix **-ar-/-al-**, which goes into the middle of a word (*balik* → *baralik* = they all go home; *geulis* → *garelis* = they're all pretty). You don't need to use the infix at A1, but you must recognize it, because you'll hear it constantly.

The words below also exist in Indonesian — the language of every sign, shop, and TV channel in West Java — but mean something different there. If you've picked up any Indonesian, they will trip you up. Those marked ⚠️ have caused real embarrassment.

blocks.title: Three sentences newcomers most often get wrong
items: ❌ *Abdi badé tuang.* → ✅ **Abdi badé neda.** — *tuang* is only for other people.
❌ *Punten, bujur teu ieu jalanna?* → ✅ **Punten, leres ieu jalanna?** — *leres* = right; *bujur* = buttocks.
❌ *Ibu tos dahar?* → ✅ **Ibu tos tuang?** — for someone you respect, use the "lemes for others" form.

blocks.text: These twenty units take you to a full A1: you can greet people at the right speech level, introduce yourself, bargain, order food, ask the way, talk about your daily life, decline politely, and read signs in the Sundanese script. Not yet: telling long stories in the past, arguing, and reading literature.
What raises your level fastest, in order

items: **Listen, don't just read.** Sundanese-language news channels (Bandung TV, TVRI Jabar) and Sundanese podcasts on YouTube give you real speaking speed. Start with the news — newsreaders are the clearest and use tidy lemes.

**Wayang golék by Asep Sunandar Sunarya.** The recordings run for hours and are free. The language is layered: Cepot the clown speaks rough, funny loma, while the knights speak high lemes. One show teaches undak usuk better than a chapter of grammar.
**Songs.** Doel Sumbang, Darso, and Nining Meida for the classics; Sunda Riut, Sisitipsi, and Mocca (their Sundanese songs) for newer ones. Sundanese lyrics are packed with everyday words.

**Use it every day, just a little.** Say **hatur nuhun** instead of "thank you", **punten** instead of "excuse me", **muhun** instead of "yes". Those three words, used consistently for a month, change how Sundanese people treat you more than a hundred words you've only memorized.

**Find one person willing to correct you.** Sundanese people are usually too polite to correct you. Ask openly: *Punten, upami abdi lepat, dibenerkeun nya* ("Excuse me — if I get it wrong, please correct me"). That sentence opens a door that won't open by itself.

blocks.text: Further reading

items: **The magazine *Mangle*** — the oldest Sundanese-language magazine still in print, a mix of news, short stories, and humor. Intermediate level.
**Folk tales**: *Sangkuriang*, *Lutung Kasarung*, *Ciung Wanara*. The children's versions use simple language and lovely wording.
**The LBSS Sundanese dictionary (Kamus Basa Sunda)** — the standard reference, including for checking a word's speech level.
**Sundanese Wikipedia (su.wikipedia.org)** — the largest free reading resource there is, and it writes the *é* mark carefully.

blocks.text: Finally, a proverb to take with you: **"Cikaracak ninggang batu, laun-laun jadi legok."** Small drops of water falling on a stone, little by little, wear a hollow in it. No language is ever mastered in one big push. *Hatur nuhun, sareng wilujeng nyarios Sunda* — thank you, and happy speaking Sundanese.
